summary.en: After the years of variety, the British Invasion begins.
summary.zh: 多样化时期过后，英伦入侵拉开了序幕。

body.zh:
欢迎来到摇滚史课程第一部分的第四章。在本章，我们将要讨论英伦入侵（British Invasion），也即The Beatles和The Rolling Stones的音乐，还有一些自1964年左右起在美国走红的歌手。

稍微重温一下我们在上一章讲的内容，算是给英伦入侵作个铺垫。因为在许多意义上，英伦入侵是对当时美国流行乐产业的一次真正冲击。所以，了解英伦入侵，十分重要。让我们快速回顾上一章的内容。我们主要谈了第一波摇滚浪潮后的景致，在此之前Elvis是最成功、最具代表性的摇滚明星。第一波浪潮自1955年持续至1959年，然后音乐行业就有点被音乐商人自己接管了，而非那些独立厂牌和独立的、确有自己想法的艺人。55至59年间，他们在青少年群体之中发现了一个极佳的、商业潜力巨大的音乐市场，于是想方设法去采掘这个金矿、制造出新的产品。这一时期的总体思路是寻找下一个Elvis，下一个能制造轰动的人。人们炮制出了很多种模样各异的流派。如我们在上章最后提到的那样，这一时期的音乐之价值如何，评论界意见不一。是过分简化、见利忘义、磨平了棱角，失去了第一波浪潮的锋利与激情；还是说，那是一个新事物井喷的黄金时代，只是被我们在本章要讲到的英伦入侵给打断了？若你是一个喜欢那类音乐的人，也许你会喜欢Sweet Soul、女子组合、制作人的崛起或是冲浪音乐，我们上回讲到的这一切。说到大众持有负面看法的东西，其中颇受针对的一样就是青少年偶像，还有舞蹈狂潮、扭扭舞。这主要是因为它们身上的肤浅性以及似乎对于青少年市场的急功近利的开发。我们讲过的其他流派还有rockabilly的传承，我将其称为rockabilly popsters，以便与55年到59年的第一代rockabilly区分开来。民谣复兴的出现也是一件大事，它让美国的青少年市场首次出现了分裂，变为少年和更年长的大学生两派；后者更喜欢民谣音乐。

虽然大家在这段时间里寻觅着下一个Elvis，但事实证明下一个Elvis不属于以上事物中的任何一类。下一个Elvis来自一个无人期许之地。下一个Elvis来自英国，而下一节我们就将讲到那时的英国是怎样一派景象、使得The Beatles和The Rolling Stones这样的乐团能够崭露头角。
body.en:
Welcome to Chapter 4 of Part One of the rock-history course. In this chapter we will discuss the British Invasion—the music of the Beatles and the Rolling Stones, and other singers who broke in the U.S. from about 1964 on.

A brief review of the last chapter helps set up the Invasion. In many senses it was a real shock to the American pop industry, so understanding it matters. We mainly covered the scene after the first rock wave, when Elvis had been the most successful and representative rock star. That first wave ran from 1955 to 1959; then the industry was somewhat taken over by the merchants themselves, rather than independent labels and independent artists with their own ideas. Between 1955 and 1959 they found an excellent teen market with huge commercial potential, and set out to mine it and manufacture new product. The overall idea was to find the next Elvis—the next person who could make a splash. Many different styles were cooked up. As we said at the end of the last chapter, critics disagree on the value of this music. Was it oversimplified, mercenary, edges sanded off, losing the bite and passion of the first wave? Or was it a golden age of new things pouring out, only interrupted by the British Invasion we cover in this chapter? If you like that music, you may like sweet soul, girl groups, the rise of the producer, or surf—everything we covered last time. Among things the public often views negatively, teen idols stand out, along with dance crazes and the Twist—mainly for their shallowness and what looks like opportunistic exploitation of the teen market. We also covered the rockabilly inheritance—what I call rockabilly popsters, to separate them from the first generation of 1955–59. The folk revival was another big event: for the first time the American teen market split into younger teens and older college students, the latter preferring folk.

While everyone hunted for the next Elvis, it turned out the next Elvis belonged to none of the above. The next Elvis came from a place no one expected—Britain. Next section we look at what Britain was like then, and how bands like the Beatles and the Rolling Stones could emerge.
